summary:
Legal gender recognition in Hungary is prohibited. Administrative refusal was already routine from 2018, and in May 2020 the Orbán government, ruling by emergency decree during the COVID-19 pandemic, pushed through a bill barring passports and identity cards from reflecting an acquired gender, including for people already legally recognised. The same bill redefined the word nem (sex) in the civil code as immutable biological sex. A trans visitor should therefore expect to enter and be documented under the marker assigned at birth, with no domestic route to correcting it.

A layer of supranational litigation runs against that domestic position. On 13 March 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled in C-247/23 (Deldits), on a reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration case, that Article 16 of the GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data once it has changed and no longer satisfies the accuracy principle of Article 5(1)(d). In September 2024 the Court's Advocate General had called on Hungarian authorities to correct the gender marker of a transgender refugee in the national registries. How far either instrument reaches a visitor's short-term documents is not established by these sources.

In April 2026 the Court of Justice found that Hungary's 2021 child-protection law, including the ban on gender change for people under 18, discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents and breached EU rules on several levels. The court held the law in breach of Article 2 of the treaty establishing the Union, an unprecedented finding against the bloc's founding values. Judgment came nine days after Hungarians voted in the 12 April 2026 election.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1961, and nothing in the entry regime conditions admission on sexual orientation or gender identity. One procedural protection does apply: in January 2018 the Court of Justice held that asylum seekers may not be subjected by authorities to psychological tests in order to determine their sexual orientation. LGBT people nevertheless continue to face discrimination and demonisation in public life, which shapes the street-level environment a visitor meets.

The 12 April 2026 election ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán's government, with Péter Magyar's Tisza party winning 138 seats. Analysts describe the outcome as a return to the democratic baseline rather than a repeal of the legal architecture built under the previous government, and Tisza has published no LGBTQ+ programme. Reform of the anti-LGBTQ statutes would require a two-thirds majority in parliament, and Tisza's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Magyar has raised questions about the pace of change. In September 2026 the new prime minister announced an intention to repeal the constitutional ban on adoption by same-sex couples.

Assembly has already reopened. The 31st Budapest Pride drew tens of thousands of marchers in June 2026, the first held since Orbán was voted out, against the backdrop of the anti-LGBT laws adopted during his rule. Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik named the restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent issue for the community. Contemporaneous reporting records cautious optimism among activists that changes will be made.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility toward LGBT people was a governing instrument for much of the previous era and forms the backdrop to the current legal position. In May 2020 the National Assembly rejected the Istanbul Convention in a resolution attacking its measures as promoting destructive gender ideologies and illegal migration; in October 2020 Orbán stated that gays are to leave our children alone. In April 2026 the Court of Justice found the 2021 child-protection law had discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents, which frames how the domestic rhetoric was received at EU level.

Defamation proceedings over that rhetoric ran their full course. After a 2021 children's book published by the Labrisz Lesbian Association, the governing party launched a smear campaign conflating homosexuality with pedophilia, and the government-linked media group Mediaworks published an article calling Labrisz pedophiles without proof. Labrisz won at first instance, but in November 2022 the Curia ruled the article had not violated its right to good reputation; the case went to the Constitutional Court. The pattern indicates weak practical recourse against anti-LGBTQ incitement in the domestic courts during that period.

Adjacent advocacy has focused on detention conditions: a 2025 national report on LGBTIQ detainees, produced by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society under an EU-funded project on the rights of LGBTIQ detainees, documents the situation of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention amid the current legal and political climate. Prospects for reform sit alongside this, since anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority and the new governing party has so far kept its position unclear.
localsOnly:
Family law for residents differs sharply from the document regime. Unregistered cohabitation has been recognised since 1996 for any couple including same-sex couples, conferring specified rights, with inheritance available only by testament and a widow's pension after ten years. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have existed since 1 July 2009 and carry the same rights as marriage except adoption, assisted reproduction and the taking of a surname. Same-sex marriage was banned by the constitution in force from 1 January 2012.

Adoption is the contested front for residents. Same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly, stepchild adoption is restricted to married different-sex couples, and a December 2020 constitutional amendment further barred adoption by same-sex couples while restricting single-parent adoption. Lesbian couples in a registered partnership have no access to IVF or donor insemination. The new prime minister announced in September 2026 an intention to repeal the ban on adoption by same-sex couples, but no repeal has been sourced here.

Residents retain no domestic route to changing legal sex, so the mismatch between identity papers and lived presentation is a standing condition of ordinary administration rather than a transitional problem. The rectification obligation recognised by the Court of Justice in C-247/23 concerns records held under the regional data-protection regulation and its application to resident registries remains governed by the Hungarian register authority.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Court of Justice's rectification ruling in C-247/23 has been implemented by the Hungarian register authority, and whether it can be invoked by a visitor rather than a resident or asylum applicant, is unresolved in the available sources. No source establishes whether the April 2026 judgment on the 2021 child-protection law has produced any change to domestic practice on gender markers, and no source confirms whether the under-18 gender-change ban remains in force pending compliance.

The inventory does not address hate-crime or hate-speech statutes covering gender identity, sentencing outcomes for violence against trans people, or any police guidance on stop-and-search or ID checks of gender-nonconforming travellers. Reporting requirements at entry, including any biometric or sex-field screening at the border, are likewise not sourced. Budapest Pride's assembly permissions for future years and any conditions attached to them are not documented beyond the June 2026 march.

The scale of the anti-LGBTQ legislative package as a whole, the parliamentary arithmetic for a two-thirds majority after the April 2026 election, and the Tisza party's actual legislative intentions on legal gender recognition are unresolved: analysts describe the election as a restoration of the democratic baseline rather than a repeal of the existing legal architecture, and no LGBTQ+ programme from Tisza has been published.
